title: लोमड़ी और खट्टे अंगूर
full_text:
एक गर्म दोपहर में एक भूखी लोमड़ी जंगल में भोजन की तलाश में भटक रही थी। घूमते-घूमते वह एक किसान के सुंदर अंगूरों के बगीचे में जा पहुँची। वहाँ एक ऊँची लकड़ी की मचान पर अंगूरों की हरी-भरी बेलें फैली हुई थीं।

बेलों पर पके हुए, रसीले और बड़े-बड़े बैंगनी अंगूरों के गुच्छे लटक रहे थे। धूप में चमकते अंगूरों को देखकर लोमड़ी के मुँह में पानी भर आया। उसने सोचा, 'अहा! आज तो भरपेट स्वादिष्ट भोजन मिलेगा!'

लोमड़ी कुछ कदम पीछे हटी, फिर दौड़कर पूरी ताक़त से ऊपर उछली, किंतु अंगूर बहुत ऊँचे थे और उसकी छलाँग अधूरी रह गई। उसने अपनी थकावट भुलाकर दूसरी बार, तीसरी बार और अनगिनत बार छलाँगें लगाईं, पर हर बार वह अंगूरों को छू भी न सकी।

जब वह पूरी तरह हाँफने लगी और उसके पैरों में शक्ति न रही, तो उसने अपनी नाक सिकोड़ी और वहाँ से मुड़ते हुए बोली, 'छी! ये अंगूर तो बिल्कुल खट्टे हैं। यदि मैं इन्हें खाऊँगी तो बीमार पड़ जाऊँगी!' और वह अपनी असफलता को छिपाने का ढोंग करते हुए चुपचाप चली गई।
moral: जो वस्तु हमें अपनी असमर्थता के कारण नहीं मिल पाती, उसमें दोष निकालना कमज़ोर मन का लक्षण है।

title: कछुआ और खरगोश की दौड़
full_text:
जंगल में एक खरगोश अपनी तीव्र गति पर बड़ा घमंड करता था। वह जब भी किसी जीव को देखता, उसकी धीमी चाल का उपहास उड़ाता। विशेष रूप से वह एक कछुए को देखकर रोज़ हँसता था, जो अपनी पीठ पर भारी खोल लिए धीरे-धीरे चलता था।

एक दिन कछुए ने तंग आकर कहा, 'खरगोश भाई! तुम भले ही हवा की तरह तेज़ दौड़ते हो, लेकिन यदि हम दोनों के बीच दौड़ हो, तो मैं तुम्हें हरा सकता हूँ!' खरगोश ठहाका मारकर हँसा और उसने चुनौती स्वीकार कर ली। लोमड़ी को दौड़ का निर्णायक बनाया गया और पहाड़ी की चोटी पर स्थित एक विशाल बरगद के पेड़ को मंज़िल तय किया गया।

दौड़ शुरू होते ही खरगोश पलक झपकते ही नज़रों से ओझल हो गया। कछुआ अपनी मंथर गति से एक-एक कदम आगे बढ़ाने लगा। आधी दूरी तय करने के बाद खरगोश ने पीछे मुड़कर देखा, कछुआ कहीं दूर-दूर तक दिखाई नहीं दे रहा था। खरगोश ने सोचा, 'कछुए को यहाँ तक आने में घंटों लगेंगे, तब तक मैं इस घने पेड़ की छाँव में थोड़ी देर सुस्ता लेता हूँ।' ठंडी हवा में उसे गहरी नींद आ गई।

इधर कछुआ बिना रुके, बिना थके लगातार चलता रहा। वह सोते हुए खरगोश के पास से चुपचाप गुज़र गया और मंज़िल तक पहुँच गया। जब खरगोश की आँख खुली, तो उसने देखा कि कछुआ विजय रेखा पार कर चुका था और सभी पशु तालियाँ बजा रहे थे। खरगोश का सिर शर्म से झुक गया।
moral: धैर्य, लगन और निरंतर प्रयास से धीमी गति वाला व्यक्ति भी घमंडी और लापरवाह को पराजित कर देता है।

title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
full_text:
Throughout the long, golden days of summer, the meadow blossomed with vibrant wildflowers, sweet clover, and rich grasses. While butterflies fluttered lazily in the warm breeze, an industrious ant worked from dawn to twilight, hauling heavy grains of wheat, seeds, and dried corn kernels back to her underground granary. She bowed her tiny shoulders beneath burdens twice her size, sweating in the heat to store food for the cold days ahead.

Perched upon a tall thistle, a merry grasshopper sang joyful melodies on his fiddle, chirping without a care in the world. Seeing the ant struggle past with a plump barley grain, he laughed dismissively: "Why do you toil so wearily under the blazing sun, little neighbor? Put down that heavy load! Summer is made for dancing, singing, and feasting on the abundance of the earth. Winter is far away; enjoy the golden hour!"

The ant wiped her brow and replied quietly, "Summer will not last forever, friend. When the frosty winds blow and snow buries the meadow, the fields will provide nothing. I advise you to gather while the sun shines." But the grasshopper laughed, shook his green antennae, and continued fiddling his carefree tunes.

Soon autumn stripped the boughs bare, and winter arrived with howling gales and deep, freezing snow. The meadow turned into a frozen, barren desert. Shivering in the icy blast, weak with hunger and without a single crumb to eat, the grasshopper crawled to the ant's snug mound. Through the doorway, he saw the ants enjoying rich stores of grain by their warm hearth.

"Have pity on me, kind neighbor!" begged the starving grasshopper. "Grant me a few morsels of your wheat, or I shall perish in the frost!"

The ant looked at him with sorrowful sternness and asked, "What did you do all through the summer when food was plentiful and the days were long?"

"Alas," wept the grasshopper, "I made sweet music and sang for all the creatures."

"If you were foolish enough to sing away the summer," answered the ant, "then you must dance away the winter," and she closed her door, leaving the idler to face the bitter fruit of his improvidence.
moral: It is best to prepare today for the inevitable needs of tomorrow.

title: The Lion and the Mouse
full_text:
A mighty lion, weary from hunting across the sun-drenched savannah, lay sleeping peacefully beneath the sprawling shade of an ancient baobab tree. His massive golden mane rippled in the breeze, and his deep snores stirred the dust around his great paws.

A timid little field mouse, scurrying through the tall grass in search of seeds, did not notice the sleeping predator and inadvertently ran straight across the lion's broad nose.

Startled from his nap, the furious king of beasts struck out with lightning speed. His heavy paw clamped down upon the tiny creature, pinning her helpless against the hard ground. Opening his cavernous jaws, the lion prepared to crush the mouse in a single bite.

"Spare me, O King!" squeaked the terrified mouse, trembling in every whisker. "I meant no disrespect! I was running blindly from a hawk. Forgive my clumsy blunder! If you grant me my life, I promise that one day I will repay your royal mercy!"

The lion let out a roar of thunderous laughter that shook the surrounding acacia branches. "Repay me? A wretched, insignificant speck of fur repay the sovereign of the forest? What an absurd fancy!" Yet, amused by her sheer boldness, the lion lifted his paw and let the tiny creature scurry safely into the rocks.

A few days later, while patrolling his territory, the lion walked into a hunter's concealed trap. Strong hemp cords snapped tight around his limbs, hoisting him helpless into a heavy rope net. The mighty beast roared in fury and thrashing anguish, but every struggle only tightened the knots.

Hearing that familiar, desperate roar echoing through the ravines, the little mouse rushed to the scene. Without hesitation, she set her sharp, needle-like teeth against the thickest cord, gnawing with frantic determination until the fibers frayed and snapped. One by one, she severed the binding ropes until the great king stepped down, completely free.

Looking down at his tiny deliverer with humble reverence, the lion bowed his great head: "You were right, little friend. Today you have taught the King of the Forest that even the smallest heart can save the mighty."
moral: No act of kindness, however small, is ever wasted; little friends may prove great allies.

title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
full_text:
A young shepherd boy was assigned the solitary task of tending a flock of sheep on a high pasture above a peaceful farming village. Day after day, he sat upon a rocky crag watching the sheep graze in silence. With no one to talk to and only the wind rustling through the gorse bushes, the boy grew thoroughly bored and longed for excitement.

Remembering his master's instructions to call for help if danger threatened, a mischievous plan took shape in his mind. He sprang to his feet, ran to the edge of the cliff overlooking the village, and shouted at the top of his lungs: "Wolf! Wolf! A ravenous wolf is attacking the flock! Help! Help!"

Down in the valley, the villagers dropped their scythes, hoes, and blacksmith hammers. Armed with pitchforks and heavy clubs, they sprinted breathlessly up the steep hill to drive the beast away and protect the sheep. When they arrived, sweating and panting, they found the flock grazing peacefully, while the boy rolled upon the grass in uncontrollable laughter at the prank.

"Do not cry wolf when there is no danger, lad!" warned the village elder sternly before trudging back down the mountain.

A few days later, the boy grew restless once more and shouted again: "Wolf! Wolf! Save the lambs!" Once again, the kind-hearted villagers rushed up the slope, only to be mocked and laughed at by the deceitful boy.

Then, one evening as the shadows lengthened and twilight enveloped the crags, a real, terrifying gray wolf emerged from the dark pine forest. Its eyes burned like fiery coals, and its dripping fangs bared in a menacing snarl as it sprang into the middle of the terrified flock, tearing at the helpless sheep.

Terrified out of his wits, the boy ran toward the cliff, waving his arms and screaming with genuine terror: "Wolf! Wolf! A giant wolf is slaughtering the sheep! I beg you, come quickly!"

Down in the village, the farmers heard his desperate cries and shook their heads. "There is that foolish boy again," said a weaver. "He will not trick us a third time; let him laugh alone."

No one came to his aid. The boy watched in weeping horror as the wolf decimated the flock and vanished into the shadows, leaving the deceitful shepherd to learn the bitter cost of destroying trust.
moral: A liar will not be believed, even when he speaks the absolute truth.

title: The Crow and the Pitcher
full_text:
A terrible drought had settled over the countryside. The streams had dried into cracked riverbeds of baked mud, the ponds had vanished, and the leaves of the olive trees drooped beneath the relentless blaze of the sun. A thirsty crow, flying for leagues in search of water, felt her throat parched like hot sand and her wings growing too heavy to beat the dry air.

As she drifted down into an abandoned courtyard, she spotted an earthenware pitcher standing upon a stone bench. With a joyous caw, the crow fluttered to the rim and peered inside. To her delight, there was clear, sparkling water at the bottom!

Eagerly, she thrust her beak into the narrow neck of the pitcher, but her bill could not reach the water. She tried to insert her head, but the vessel's neck was too tight. In desperation, she attempted to push the pitcher over with her breast, hoping to spill the water onto the stone slab and drink from the puddle, but the heavy clay container was far too sturdy for her slender strength.

Weeping with frustration, the crow rested upon the bench, refusing to give up. Her keen black eyes noticed a pile of smooth river pebbles scattered near the courtyard fountain. A brilliant spark of ingenuity flashed in her mind.

Taking a smooth pebble in her beak, she flew up and dropped it into the pitcher: plunk! The water level rose an imperceptible fraction. She flew down, took a second pebble, and dropped it in: plunk! Then a third, a fourth, a fifth, and a sixth.

Dozens of times the patient bird flew back and forth in the blazing heat, never flagging in her resolve. With every stone dropped into the dark vessel, the cool water steadily mounted toward the rim. At last, the liquid reached the very top of the neck. The triumphant crow dipped her bill and drank long, refreshing draughts of cool water, saving her life through patient intellect and steady perseverance.
moral: Little by little does the trick; intelligence and patience solve problems that force cannot.

title: The Fox and the Crow
full_text:
A glossy black crow had swooped down onto an open farmhouse windowsill and snatched a magnificent wedge of rich, yellow Swiss cheese. Delighted with her delicious prize, she flew up into the high branches of an ancient oak tree, intending to feast upon it in undisturbed peace.

A crafty fox, wandering through the woods in search of breakfast, caught the rich aroma of aged cheese drifting on the morning breeze. He followed his keen nose to the foot of the oak and looked up into the leafy canopy. Seeing the crow perched high above with the plump morsel held firmly in her beak, his mouth watered with desire.

The fox sat gracefully upon his haunches, tilted his head, and addressed the bird in a voice as smooth as melted butter: "Good morning, most radiant mistress Crow! How breathtakingly beautiful your plumage gleams in the morning sunlight! Your feathers possess a sheen finer than the finest velvet, and your graceful eyes sparkle like black diamonds. Surely, a queen of such peerless beauty must also possess a voice of celestial sweetness! If you would only sing one song for your humble admirer, I would gladly proclaim you sovereign of all winged creatures!"

The foolish crow was swept away by this lavish praise. Puffing out her chest and fluttering her wings with vanity, she resolved to prove that she was indeed the greatest singer of the forest.

She opened her beak wide and let out a harsh, rasping "Caw-w-w!"

The moment her beak parted, the heavy wedge of cheese slipped from her grasp and tumbled straight down through the branches. The nimble fox leaped forward, caught the delicious morsel in mid-air, and swallowed it in a single greedy gulp.

Licking his lips with satisfaction, the fox looked up at the mortified bird and laughed: "My dear mistress, your voice is as wretched as your feathers are dark. The song was clumsy, but the cheese was divine! In return for your meal, take this valuable advice: never trust anyone who flatters you for their own gain!"
moral: Never trust a flatterer who praises you to rob you of your prize.

title: The Goose That Laid the Golden Eggs
full_text:
A humble peasant and his wife lived in a modest cottage on the outskirts of town, subsisting on the meager vegetables grown in their garden and the milk of a solitary goat. One morning, the peasant walked into the poultry shed to gather eggs and noticed an extraordinary gleam beneath an old gray goose.

Reaching into the straw, he pulled out an egg that felt astonishingly heavy. When he wiped away the dust, the egg shone with the warm, brilliant luster of solid gold! Trembling with disbelief, he carried it to a goldsmith in the town, who weighed it and handed him a bag of silver coins, confirming it was pure, unalloyed gold.

Every morning thereafter, the miraculous goose laid another solid golden egg. The peasant and his wife quickly sold the eggs, bought fine velvet garments, built a luxurious manor house, and hired servants to attend their every whim.

Yet as their wealth expanded, an insatiable greed took root in their hearts. They grew impatient with receiving only one golden egg each morning. "Why should we wait day after day for a single egg?" whispered the greedy wife over dinner. "Inside that bird there must surely be a vast mountain of pure gold! If we cut her open, we can seize the entire treasury all at once and become richer than the king before nightfall!"

Blinded by covetousness, the peasant seized a heavy carving knife and slaughtered the miraculous goose. But when he cut the bird open, to his utter horror, her internal organs were identical in every way to those of an ordinary farmyard fowl! There was no hidden store of gold within.

The foolish couple fell to their knees in weeping despair. In their blind greed to possess everything at once, they had slain the gentle creature that provided their fortune, leaving themselves with only regret and the bitter memory of what they had squandered.
moral: Greed that seeks all at once destroys the very source of steady prosperity.

title: The Wind and the Sun
full_text:
A fierce argument arose between the North Wind and the Sun as to which of them possessed greater strength and power over the earth. The North Wind puffed out his icy cheeks and roared with blustering arrogance: "I am the undisputed master of might! I uproot ancient oaks with my breath, stir the oceans into mountainous waves, and strip mountains bare with icy blasts. You do nothing but shine softly like a sleepy lantern!"

The Sun smiled with serene, radiant warmth and replied gently, "True power does not lie in violent noise or harsh destruction, brother. Let us put our strength to a fair test."

Looking down through the drifting clouds, they saw a solitary traveler walking along a winding mountain highway, wrapped in a thick, woolen traveler's cloak against the autumn chill.

"Whoever can compel that traveler to remove his cloak," said the Sun, "shall be acknowledged as the mightier of the two."

"A simple task!" boomed the North Wind. "Watch and marvel!"

The North Wind unleashed his fury. He whistled down from the icy polar heights, howling with hurricane force and driving freezing gusts of sleet against the lone traveler. Leaves tore from the branches, and dust swirled in blinding storms. But the harder the fierce wind blew, the tighter the shivering traveler grasped his cloak, wrapping it doubly around his chest and pinning the collar beneath his chin. Furious, the Wind redoubled his tempest, but he only succeeded in wearying himself, leaving the man wrapped more securely than before.

At last, exhausted and defeated, the North Wind ceased his gale.

Then the Sun stepped out from behind a silver cloud. He sent forth gentle, golden rays that bathed the rugged hills in soft, soothing warmth. The chilly moisture evaporated, flowers lifted their heads, and the traveler felt the pleasant glow spreading across his tired shoulders.

As the Sun shone brighter with increasing radiance, the traveler unbuttoned his collar, wiped the beads of sweat from his forehead, and finally unclasped the heavy woolen cloak altogether, draping it over his arm and strolling merrily on his way under the pleasant sunshine. The humbled Wind was forced to concede that gentle kindness overcomes what fury fails to move.
moral: Gentle warmth and persuasion accomplish what fierce force and bluster never can.

title: The Wolf in Sheep's Clothing
full_text:
A cunning wolf had long hungered after the fat, tender sheep of a well-guarded pasture, but the alert shepherd and his ferocious mastiffs watched over the flock so vigilantly that the predator could never draw near without being driven off with stones and sharp spears.

Prowling around the edge of the farm one evening, the wolf discovered the complete fleece of a sheep that had been sheared and discarded by the shearers. A wicked scheme flashed in his devious mind.

"If I cannot approach as a hunter," whispered the wolf, "I shall enter as a brother."

He draped the soft, woolly skin carefully over his back, tucking his sharp snout beneath the fleece and mimicking the gentle bleat of a lamb. Disguised in snowy innocence, he strolled casually into the green pasture among the flock.

The sheep, suspecting nothing from a creature wearing wool, accepted him in their midst. Even the shepherd failed to spot the predator among his charges. When night fell, the shepherd gathered the flock into the stout wooden fold, bolted the heavy oak gate, and went to his cottage for supper, leaving the wolf locked safely inside with his intended prey.

The wolf licked his fangs, chuckling softly in the dark at how easily he had outwitted the dogs, planning to slaughter a plump lamb the moment everyone fell asleep.

Later that night, the shepherd's cook was sent out to the sheepfold with a lantern to butcher a sheep for the master's banquet the following morning. Moving through the dark pen, the cook reached blindly for the first large, heavy beast he felt in the shadows. His hand grasped the wolf in sheep's fleece. Before the predator could realize what was happening, the butcher's knife ended his life on the spot, demonstrating that those who disguise themselves in false innocence often perish by the very trap they laid.
moral: He who wears a mask of innocence to deceive others falls into the snare of his own disguise.

title: The Dog and the Bone
full_text:
A butcher had tossed a juicy, marrow-filled bone to a mastiff who lingered outside the shop. Proud of his delicious prize, the dog clamped his jaws firmly around the bone and trotted off toward his home across the river, eager to enjoy his feast in quiet solitude.

As he crossed a narrow wooden footbridge over a clear, tranquil stream, he happened to look down into the mirror-like surface of the water. There, gazing back up at him from the depths, he beheld another dog holding a bone that appeared twice as large and plump as his own!

Unaware that he was looking at his own reflection, the greedy dog was seized with an overwhelming desire to possess the second prize. "Why should I settle for one bone," he thought, "when I can easily snatch that larger one and enjoy a double banquet?"

Snarling with aggressive greed, he opened his jaws wide to snap at the rival in the stream.

The moment his teeth parted, his own precious bone slipped from his mouth, plunged into the rushing water with a splash, and sank straight to the muddy bottom, carried away by the current.

The startled dog stared down into the ripples, seeing the reflection now empty-mouthed like himself. Whimpering with regret and an empty belly, he trudged home, having learned too late that insatiable greed sacrifices present abundance for worthless illusions.
moral: He who grasps at shadows loses the real substance of what he holds.

title: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
full_text:
A humble Country Mouse who lived in an underground burrow beneath the roots of a wild hazel bush invited his aristocratic cousin, the Town Mouse, to visit him for dinner. The Country Mouse, proud of his hospitality, served the best provisions his pantry could afford: dried wheat stalks, wild berry seeds, and a hard crust of barley bread.

The Town Mouse turned up his whiskers with polite disdain, merely nibbling a seed or two. "My dear cousin," drawled the elegant visitor, "how can you endure such a dreary, monotonous existence among roots and chaff? Come with me to the grand city mansion where I reside! You shall dine upon rich cheeses, sweet pastries, and roasted meats fit for kings."

Enticed by visions of royal luxury, the Country Mouse accompanied his cousin to the city. That night, they crept into the mansion's vast dining hall, where a lavish banquet had just concluded. title: The Frogs Who Desired a King

The frogs of a wide, fertile marsh lived in blissful freedom, leaping through the reeds, sunning themselves on water lilies, and croaking in noisy chorus whenever they pleased. But over time, they grew dissatisfied with their orderly liberty. "Every kingdom on earth has a sovereign to rule over them," they argued. "Why should we be a leaderless rabble? They sent a solemn petition to the heavens, begging for a king to rule over them.

Amused by their foolishness, Jupiter tossed a colossal wooden log down into the center of the swamp. It struck the water with a tremendous splash: CRASH! Gradually, seeing the monarch neither moved nor spoke, a bold frog poked his head above the water. Seeing only an inert piece of timber floating among the duckweed, the frogs swam closer. Within an hour, they were leaping onto the log, sunning on its bark, and mocking its total silence.

"This is no king!" they croaked in indignation. "It is a lifeless, contemptible stick! We demand a dynamic, vigorous ruler who commands respect and takes action!"

Wearied by their incessant complaining, Jupiter sent them a tall, long-legged Water Stork.

The moment the new sovereign landed in the marsh, he strode through the shallows with his sharp, spear-like beak, gobbling down the frogs one by one! The terrified survivors hid in deep crevices, weeping and praying to have their gentle log returned. But the heavens answered: "You rejected peaceful freedom and despised a gentle ruler; now you must endure the tyrant you so foolishly demanded."

title: The Wolf and the Lamb

title: The Miser

A watchful laborer, noticing the miser's daily pilgrimages and suspicious demeanor, trailed him to the woods. The moment the old man departed, the laborer dug into the loose dirt, unearthed the colossal nugget of gold, and carried it off to enjoy its fortune.

"My gold! My life's treasure!" shrieked the miser. "I buried a giant lump of gold in this very spot, and a vile thief has stolen it away!"

"Did you ever spend any of it?" asked the neighbor. "Did you buy food, help your family, or purchase warm clothes?"

title: The Dog and the Wolf

A gaunt, starving wolf, whose ribs showed through his matted gray fur after weeks of harsh winter blizzards, happened to meet a plump, sleek house dog strolling along the edge of a village lane. The mastiff was glossy, round-bellied, and radiated robust health.

"Oh, that is nothing," answered the dog casually. "It is merely the mark of the iron collar and chain with which they tie me up during the daytime, so that I do not wander off or bite the visitors. But at night they set me free!"

The wolf stopped dead in his tracks. His amber eyes widened. "Tie you up?" he echoed. "Do you mean you cannot roam the forests whenever you please?"

"Not by day," admitted the dog. "But what does that matter when food is abundant?"

"It matters everything," declared the wolf, backing into the shadows of the woods. "Enjoy your fat bones, cousin, and your comfortable kennel. I would rather starve as a free wanderer than grow fat as a pampered slave in chains!" And he sprinted back into the wild freedom of the wilderness.

title: The Horse and the Ass

A country peddler was traveling to the city market with his two beasts of burden: a proud, sleek warhorse adorned with brass-studded harness, and a patient, humble little donkey. Staggering beneath the crushing weight, his back groaning under the double burden, the horse groaned in bitter remorse: "Alas, what a fool I was! By refusing to help my brother with a small sack, I am now forced to carry his entire load and his skin into the bargain!"

title: The Fox and the Woodcutter
full_text:
A fox, breathless and exhausted from a long pursuit by royal hounds, burst into a clearing where an honest woodcutter was chopping pine logs. The fox fell upon his knees and begged: "Have mercy, woodcutter! Hide me in your cottage, I implore you, or the hounds will tear me apart!"

The woodcutter pointed toward his rustic hut and promised to protect him. The fox dashed inside and crouched beneath a pile of dry faggots.

A moment later, the huntsmen arrived on foaming horses. "Woodcutter!" shouted the captain. "Did a fox pass this way?"

"No, I have seen no fox!" shouted the woodcutter with a loud, honest voice. But at the very same moment, he slyly pointed his thumb toward the door of his cottage, winking at the hunters.

The huntsmen, listening only to his words and ignoring his gesture, galloped past down the road.

When the danger had passed, the fox emerged from the hut and trotted off into the woods without uttering a single word of thanks.

"Where is your gratitude?" called the woodcutter indignantly. "I saved your skin, and you leave without a polite farewell!"

The fox turned around and replied: "I would have thanked you with all my heart if your fingers had agreed with your tongue, and if your deeds had not contradicted your speech!"
moral: Hypocrisy that swears faith with words while betraying with deeds is contemptible.
